title: Morning Edition
notes: Morning Edition for Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026. Covers news since the Nov 27 morning edition.

Leading this morning: the Supreme Court of Canada’s ruling upholding almost all of Quebec’s Bill 21. Also: the American Airlines wing clip at Reagan National, OpenAI’s countersuit against Apple, Black Friday online spending, the USWNT’s World Cup berth and Inter Miami’s playoff exit, the rescheduled Macy’s parade, the CRTC’s ruling on phone fees, Kenneth Law’s sentencing hearing, the Blue Jays’ Taira and Chisholm deals, the Mackenzie Valley Highway, Hong Kong’s flag-desecration ruling, the SmartPLAY and Octopus data breaches, the Central Kowloon Bypass opening date, the posthumous bravery medal for a Tai Po firefighter, Taiwan’s local elections (partial count), China’s industrial profits, the Shenzhou crew handover, a BBC report on exiled activists, Victoria’s election, the Kunar school explosion, the Shakahola manslaughter verdict, the strike on an MSF clinic in Gaza and Marc Márquez’s retirement.

Updates on earlier stories: Bill 21 (Nov 26 and Nov 27 editions reported the ruling was scheduled), Black Friday (Nov 27 edition reported forecasts), Kaima Taira (Nov 25 edition reported the agreement before it was official), the Macy’s parade postponement (Nov 26–27), the Tai Po fire anniversary (Nov 27) and Shenzhou-24 (Nov 25–26).

Planned or scheduled, not confirmed when this edition was prepared: the rescheduled Macy’s parade (Saturday, Nov. 28), Canada’s CONCACAF W Championship quarterfinal against Panama (Saturday, Nov. 28), Shenzhou-23’s return (“in the coming days”), Marc Márquez’s final race in Valencia (Sunday, Nov. 29), Taira’s introduction in Toronto (Monday, Nov. 30), the Central Kowloon Bypass opening (Sunday, Dec. 6) and the CRTC’s Dec. 27 deadline. Spain’s general election (Sunday, Nov. 29) is not covered as a story because it has not happened yet. Taiwan and Victoria results were partial; Black Friday totals are industry estimates.

Photos appear on the lead and on 13 of 22 other stories. All are file photos of the people, places or kinds of scenes involved, not of the events reported here. Text-only where no suitable openly licensed photo was found or a photo would be inappropriate: the CRTC ruling, the Kenneth Law hearing, Black Friday spending, China’s industrial profits, the Shenzhou handover, the BBC activists report, the Kunar explosion, the Shakahola verdict and the MSF clinic strike.

Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 4, China 4, World 5. Hong Kong and China have four each: other candidates found this morning were minor (a contained scaffolding fire in Tuen Mun), already covered, or rested on a single report, so the sections were not padded. Several stories rest partly on unnamed sources, company or industry figures, state media or a single outlet; this is noted under each story’s sources.
provenance: Compiled from the linked reporting, official releases and documents listed under each story; labels show whether a point is reported, an official statement, a claim, an allegation or rests on unnamed sources or state media.

Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:17 AM and 6:26 AM ET on Nov 28; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched. Photo licences were read from each Wikimedia Commons file page’s metadata in the same session.

Xinhua is Chinese state media; Focus Taiwan is the English service of Taiwan’s state-owned Central News Agency; RTHK is Hong Kong’s government-funded broadcaster; ABC and SBS are Australian public broadcasters. Wire copy carried by another outlet is marked with the agency’s name.

Access limits: the Guardian, Reuters (directly and via Investing.com), Arab News and the CRTC’s decision page refused automated fetches this morning, so they are not cited. These are access limits, not evidence of errors.

Figures differ between sources on the Kunar explosion casualties (BBC: 7 dead, 99 injured; AP: 7 and 90+; Al Jazeera: 6 and 97), the Jazz Chisholm Jr. contract (AP: US$34.5 million over two seasons; MLB.com: one year, US$20 million with options) and Black Friday online sales (Adobe and Salesforce use different methods); each is noted in the story.

stories.dateLabel: Ruling Nov 27, 2026 (update to the Nov 26 and Nov 27 editions)
stories.headline: Supreme Court of Canada upholds almost all of Quebec’s religious-symbols ban, striking only its application to elected members
stories.deck: Canada’s top court on Friday, Nov. 27, upheld nearly all of Quebec’s Bill 21, the 2019 secularism law that bars teachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work. The one exception: the ban cannot apply to members of Quebec’s National Assembly, because that would infringe elected officials’ democratic rights.
stories.summary: Canada’s top court on Friday, Nov. 27, upheld nearly all of Quebec’s Bill 21, the 2019 secularism law that bars teachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work. The one exception: the ban cannot apply to members of Quebec’s National Assembly, because that would infringe elected officials’ democratic rights. “Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” Chief Justice Richard Wagner wrote, according to CBC News. Quebec shielded the law with the Charter’s notwithstanding clause, which lets legislatures override some rights for renewable five-year periods; the court upheld that use. CBC reports the seven judges dismissed all the appeals and split 4–3 on whether the law violates the Charter’s guarantee of equality between the sexes (Section 28), with three dissenters saying it does; the BBC reports the court also said courts may still declare whether a law is consistent with the Charter even when the clause is invoked, but declined to do so here. Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon called the ruling “a victory for secularism,” AP reported. Prime Minister Mark Carney said he respected the decision and, per AP, pledged his government would not use the override; Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew called Bill 21 “legislative racism.” The National Council of Canadian Muslims called the law discriminatory.
stories.why: The ruling gives every province a clearer green light to use the notwithstanding clause pre-emptively, so the fight over religious symbols and minority rights now moves from the courts to politics: future elections, the clause’s five-year renewals and possible copycat laws elsewhere. For teachers and others who wear a hijab, turban, kippah or cross, the job restrictions in Quebec stay in place.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Follows the Nov 26 and Nov 27 editions, which reported that the ruling was scheduled. Outlets describe the judges’ splits differently because the court answered about ten separate questions with different majorities; this summary uses CBC’s account of the 4–3 split on Section 28. The ruling itself was not read in full for this edition.

stories.dateLabel: Decision Nov 27, 2026; fees must stop by Dec 27, 2026
stories.headline: CRTC orders Bell, Rogers and Telus to stop charging phone set-up and SIM fees by Dec. 27, and weighs a fine for Bell
stories.deck: Canada’s telecom regulator ruled on Friday, Nov. 27, that a Bell cellphone handling charge, a Rogers set-up charge and a Telus SIM and eSIM provisioning fee break the Telecommunications Act, and ordered the companies to stop charging them by Dec. 27.
stories.summary: Canada’s telecom regulator ruled on Friday, Nov. 27, that a Bell cellphone handling charge, a Rogers set-up charge and a Telus SIM and eSIM provisioning fee break the Telecommunications Act, and ordered the companies to stop charging them by Dec. 27. The CRTC also found that a provider broke consumer rules by selling phones locked to its network for up to 60 days and will consider a penalty of up to $10 million; CBC News identifies that provider as Bell. Fees Rogers and Telus charge to replace lost or broken SIM cards, and Rogers’ shipping fees, were found to be allowed. The CRTC said it acted after learning consumers were still being charged extra fees after earlier rules took effect.
stories.why: Device and SIM fees are small individually but are charged on almost every new plan, so ending them makes switching carriers cheaper — which is the point of the rules. Whether Bell is actually fined will show how hard the regulator is prepared to push.

stories.headline: Kenneth Law apologizes to victims’ families as Crown seeks 25 years and defence asks for 12
stories.deck: Kenneth Law, the Ontario man who sold potentially deadly substances online to people who used them to end their lives, apologized in a Newmarket, Ont., courtroom on Friday, Nov. 27, calling his actions “categorically wrong.”
stories.summary: Kenneth Law, the Ontario man who sold potentially deadly substances online to people who used them to end their lives, apologized in a Newmarket, Ont., courtroom on Friday, Nov. 27, calling his actions “categorically wrong.” “To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones,” he said, according to The Canadian Press. Law, 61, pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in Ontario. Prosecutors asked for a 25-year sentence, arguing money was his motive; his lawyers proposed 12 years minus credit for time served, saying he was misguided rather than a “mercenary predator.” He has been linked to dozens of deaths worldwide, including 79 in the United Kingdom that are being considered at sentencing; the BBC reports he will not face charges in the UK under a plea deal in which more serious Canadian murder charges were withdrawn.
stories.why: No Canadian court has sentenced a case like this, so the judge’s decision will set a benchmark for online sales of lethal substances. Families in Canada and Britain are watching whether the sentence reflects deaths far beyond the 14 charged.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: If you or someone you know is struggling, in Canada call or text 9-8-8; in the U.S. call or text 988. The sources checked did not give a date for the sentencing decision.

stories.headline: Blue Jays make Kaima Taira’s five-year deal official and reportedly agree with Jazz Chisholm Jr.
stories.deck: The Toronto Blue Jays on Friday, Nov. 27, announced a five-year, US$80-million contract with Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira, first reported earlier in the week. Hours later, several outlets reported the club had also agreed to terms with former Yankees infielder-outfielder Jazz Chisholm Jr.
stories.summary: The Toronto Blue Jays on Friday, Nov. 27, announced a five-year, US$80-million contract with Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira, first reported earlier in the week. Taira is to be introduced at a news conference on Monday, Nov. 30. Hours later, several outlets reported the club had also agreed to terms with former Yankees infielder-outfielder Jazz Chisholm Jr., a two-time all-star who stole a career-high 41 bases this season. The Blue Jays had not confirmed the Chisholm deal. Reported terms differ: the Associated Press, citing two people familiar with the talks, said it guarantees US$34.5 million over two seasons, while MLB.com, citing a source, described a one-year, US$20-million deal with a player option for 2028 that could lead to a larger club option. MLB.com notes Toronto finished last in the AL East at 79–83 and had the majors’ lowest-scoring offence.
stories.why: After a last-place season, Toronto is spending early and leaning into the Japanese market alongside Kazuma Okamoto. Chisholm would add speed to the weakest lineup in baseball — but until the team confirms it, treat the contract details as reported, not final.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported + Unnamed sources
stories.note: Follows the Nov 25 edition, which reported the Taira agreement before it was official. The Chisholm deal rests on unnamed sources, and the reported figures differ by outlet.

stories.headline: Carney lists the Mackenzie Valley Highway as the North’s first ‘project of national interest’
stories.deck: Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday, Nov. 27, listed the long-proposed Mackenzie Valley Highway in the Northwest Territories as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act, the first in Canada’s North, to speed up federal approvals.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday, Nov. 27, listed the long-proposed Mackenzie Valley Highway in the Northwest Territories as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act, the first in Canada’s North, to speed up federal approvals. The planned 800-kilometre all-season road would link Highway 1 at Wrigley to the Dempster Highway near Inuvik, reducing reliance on seasonal barges and winter roads that a warming climate has made less predictable. The Prime Minister’s Office says the designation respects Aboriginal and treaty rights and the treaty-based assessment process under the Mackenzie Valley Resource Management Act. CBC News reports construction could begin as early as late 2027; federal, territorial and Indigenous leaders signed a governance agreement in Yellowknife. Versions of the highway have been studied for nearly 70 years, and it has faced Indigenous opposition before land-claim settlements, community worries about drugs and crime, and rising costs.
stories.why: An all-season road would change the cost of living and supply in communities such as Norman Wells and Fort Good Hope, and Ottawa is pitching it as Arctic sovereignty too. The designation speeds paperwork, not geography: cost, permafrost and the territorial review still decide when — or whether — it gets built.

stories.headline: Two American Airlines jets clip wingtips while taxiing at Reagan National; no injuries, FAA to investigate
stories.deck: Two American Airlines Boeing 737-800s touched wingtips while taxiing for departure at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport at about 5:10 p.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 27, the Federal Aviation Administration said. No one was hurt.
stories.summary: Two American Airlines Boeing 737-800s touched wingtips while taxiing for departure at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport at about 5:10 p.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 27, the Federal Aviation Administration said. No one was hurt. The FAA said Flight 638, bound for Dallas-Fort Worth, clipped the wing of Flight 2152, bound for Chicago O’Hare; both planes returned to the gate and were taken out of service for inspection, and the FAA said it would investigate. On air-traffic-control audio reported by CNN, one pilot said they had “swapped paint” with the plane beside them, and a winglet was broken off; another arriving flight was told to abort its landing. A passenger told the BBC the plane “shook quite violently.” American said passengers would be rebooked. The airport is where 67 people died in a midair collision between a jetliner and an Army helicopter in January 2025.
stories.why: Ground collisions are usually minor, but this one happened at one of the country’s most congested airports, already under scrutiny since the 2025 crash, on one of the busiest travel weekends of the year. The FAA’s findings on how two jets ended up that close will matter more than the dented metal.

stories.headline: OpenAI countersues Apple, accusing it of taking OpenAI device secrets and pressuring suppliers; Apple calls it a distraction
stories.deck: OpenAI filed counterclaims against Apple in federal court in San Jose, California, on Friday, Nov. 27, alleging that Apple obtained confidential information about an unreleased OpenAI device and pressured shared suppliers not to work on OpenAI hardware.
stories.summary: OpenAI filed counterclaims against Apple in federal court in San Jose, California, on Friday, Nov. 27, alleging that Apple obtained confidential information about an unreleased OpenAI device and pressured shared suppliers not to work on OpenAI hardware. The filing answers Apple’s July lawsuit accusing OpenAI and its hardware chief Tang Tan of a campaign to steal Apple trade secrets through recruits. According to Bloomberg’s account of the filing, OpenAI says a former employee who returned to Apple sent more than a hundred confidential files about at least one unreleased OpenAI device to personal accounts, and that suppliers moved or rescheduled meetings to avoid Apple seeing them — one shifting OpenAI work to a night shift. OpenAI is also challenging Apple’s employment agreements, including a one-year ban on recruiting former colleagues. Apple called the counterclaims “a transparent attempt to distract” from its case, in which, it said, OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple’s confidential information.
stories.why: The two companies used to be partners on ChatGPT in the iPhone; now they are fighting over who gets the engineers and factories for the next AI gadget. Everything here is allegation on both sides, but the supplier claims could draw antitrust interest if a court finds Apple squeezed a rival out of shared factories.
stories.label: Allegation + Reported
stories.note: These are allegations in court filings; none has been proven. Reuters’ report could not be opened (access limit).

stories.headline: Black Friday online spending runs ahead of forecasts, Adobe says, on track for $13 billion or more
stories.deck: U.S. shoppers spent $9.7 billion online on Black Friday through 6:30 p.m. ET on Nov. 27, up 12.8% from the same point last year, according to Adobe Analytics, which now expects the day to finish between $13 billion and $13.4 billion — above its September forecast of $12.9 billion.
stories.summary: U.S. shoppers spent $9.7 billion online on Black Friday through 6:30 p.m. ET on Nov. 27, up 12.8% from the same point last year, according to Adobe Analytics, which now expects the day to finish between $13 billion and $13.4 billion — above its September forecast of $12.9 billion. Adobe said Thanksgiving Day online sales rose 10.4% to a record $7.1 billion. It forecasts $6.1 billion on Saturday, $6.4 billion on Sunday and $15.1 billion on Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, for $47.5 billion across the five days. Salesforce, which measures differently, projected $18.7 billion in U.S. Black Friday online sales, up 4%.
stories.why: Online spending growing faster than expected suggests shoppers are still spending despite inflation worries, though much of it is chasing discounts. These are industry tallies of online sales only, not total retail; the government’s figures come later.
stories.label: Industry figures + Reported
stories.note: Follows the Nov 27 edition, which reported the forecasts before Black Friday. Adobe and Salesforce use different data and methods, so their totals are not comparable. stories.headline: USWNT books a 2027 World Cup place with 8–0 rout of El Salvador; Columbus knocks Messi’s Inter Miami out of the playoffs
stories.deck: Ashley Sanchez scored a first-half hat trick as the United States beat El Salvador 8–0 in Mansfield, Texas, on Friday, Nov. 27, winning a CONCACAF W Championship quarterfinal and a place at the 2027 Women’s World Cup in Brazil.
stories.summary: Ashley Sanchez scored a first-half hat trick as the United States beat El Salvador 8–0 in Mansfield, Texas, on Friday, Nov. 27, winning a CONCACAF W Championship quarterfinal and a place at the 2027 Women’s World Cup in Brazil. The U.S. meets Jamaica, which also qualified with a 3–0 win over Costa Rica, in the semifinals; Canada plays Panama and Mexico plays Haiti in the remaining quarterfinals on Saturday, Nov. 28, with all four winners earning World Cup berths. In MLS, the Columbus Crew eliminated defending champions Inter Miami and Lionel Messi on Friday: Santiago Rodríguez scored in the 92nd minute for a 1–0 win that completed a two-game sweep of their best-of-three first-round series. Columbus faces New England or Philadelphia in the Eastern Conference semifinals on Dec. 5–6.
stories.why: For the U.S. women, qualifying early takes pressure off a rebuilding squad and leaves a year to settle a lineup for Brazil. For MLS, losing its biggest star in the first round dents playoff ratings and raises fresh questions about Miami’s ageing core.

stories.headline: Macy’s 100th parade is set to march on Saturday after the storm delay, as visiting bands scramble to cover extra days in New York
stories.deck: The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, postponed for the first time in its history because of the Thanksgiving storm, is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 28 — leaving hundreds of touring performers to rearrange travel and pay for extra nights in New York.
stories.summary: The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, postponed for the first time in its history because of the Thanksgiving storm, is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 28 — leaving hundreds of touring performers to rearrange travel and pay for extra nights in New York. The BBC reports that the director of Texas’s Pearland High School band, with more than 500 people on the trip, launched a fundraiser that raised $350,000 within hours; some performers reportedly had to skip the parade. Organizers announced the postponement on Wednesday afternoon, partly over concerns about the giant balloons in strong winds; the parade was suspended altogether during World War II but had never been postponed. NPR reports some new balloons are set to fly; executive producer Will Coss told NPR organizers wanted to do everything they could so student musicians could stay in New York and march.
stories.why: The parade is a TV ritual for millions, but for school bands it is often a once-in-a-lifetime trip paid for with bake sales — a weather delay can cost them thousands. Saturday’s forecast and crowds will show how well New York absorbs a rescheduled mega-event.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Planned event: whether the parade went ahead as scheduled had not been reported when this edition was prepared. Follows the Nov 26 and Nov 27 editions, which reported the postponement.

stories.headline: Hong Kong’s top court quashes an autistic man’s flag-desecration convictions, saying intent to insult was never proved
stories.deck: Hong Kong’s Court of Final Appeal on Friday, Nov. 27, unanimously quashed the convictions of a young man with autism for desecrating the national and Hong Kong flags, ruling the prosecution never proved he intended to insult the flags as symbols.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Court of Final Appeal on Friday, Nov. 27, unanimously quashed the convictions of a young man with autism for desecrating the national and Hong Kong flags, ruling the prosecution never proved he intended to insult the flags as symbols. Wong Chun-lok, then 19, pulled down one national flag and four regional flags in Sham Shui Po on National Day in 2022 by bending their flagpoles, and was sentenced to a rehabilitation centre. He was diagnosed with autism at three and also has ADHD and hypersensitivity to visual stimuli; his mother testified about a similar 2018 incident in which he pulled down shop banners that disturbed him. Delivering the judgment, Justice Joseph Fok held that both offences require proof of intent to undermine the flag’s dignity as a symbol — recklessness is not enough — and called the earlier appeal judge’s analysis “wholly inadequate,” RTHK reported.
stories.why: Flag offences are politically charged in Hong Kong, so a unanimous ruling that prosecutors must prove deliberate intent sets a clear limit on how the law can be applied — especially to people whose disabilities explain their actions. It is a reminder that the top court can still check lower courts on the facts.

stories.headline: Two Hong Kong data breaches in a day: government sports-booking system SmartPLAY and Octopus disclose cyberattacks
stories.deck: Hong Kong’s Leisure and Cultural Services Department said on Friday, Nov. 27, that hackers had reached personal data linked to about 90,000 old Leisure Link accounts through its SmartPLAY sports-booking system. Hours later, Octopus said a cyberattack had exposed data on about 7,500 customers and 22,000 merchants.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Leisure and Cultural Services Department said on Friday, Nov. 27, that hackers had reached personal data linked to about 90,000 old Leisure Link accounts through its SmartPLAY sports-booking system. Hours later, Octopus said a cyberattack had exposed data on about 7,500 customers and 22,000 merchants. The LCSD said preliminary findings show the intrusion came through SmartPLAY’s “Reactivate Leisure Link Account” function, reported by its contractor on Nov. 26; the data involved dates of birth, phone numbers, addresses, gender and email addresses, plus names of about 1,500 users, but no identity-document or payment details. The privacy commissioner has opened an investigation, and password recovery has been suspended. Octopus said it detected the attack on the morning of Nov. 27 and contained it; customer names and photographs were affected, and for some Automatic Add Value Service users, bank codes and top-up amounts, but no credit-card or bank-account information. It said core services were running normally and it had found no customer financial loss.
stories.why: SmartPLAY and Octopus are part of daily life for millions of Hong Kongers, and leaked names, numbers and photos are exactly what scammers use to sound convincing. Expect a wave of phishing calls and messages; the privacy watchdog is urging people to stop and think before sharing details or paying anyone who contacts them, even if the caller knows their personal information.

stories.summary: The last section of Hong Kong’s Central Kowloon Bypass — a 3.4-kilometre Kowloon Bay link that is mostly tunnel — is scheduled to open at 7 a.m. on Sunday, Dec. 6, completing the 12.5-kilometre Route 6 across Kowloon, the government said on Friday, Nov. 27. stories.headline: Firefighter who died in the Wang Fuk Court blaze receives Hong Kong’s Gold Medal for Bravery; official says the site’s future may take years
stories.deck: Senior fireman Ho Wai-ho, who died fighting last November’s Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po, was awarded the Medal for Bravery (Gold) posthumously on Saturday, Nov. 28, at Government House; his brother and fiancée accepted it from Chief Executive John Lee.
stories.summary: Senior fireman Ho Wai-ho, who died fighting last November’s Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po, was awarded the Medal for Bravery (Gold) posthumously on Saturday, Nov. 28, at Government House; his brother and fiancée accepted it from Chief Executive John Lee, and the room applauded for about half a minute, RTHK reported. The government said 302 people received honours on the first day of the two-day ceremony, including three Grand Bauhinia Medals — RTHK names Executive Council member Chan Kin-por, economist Lawrence Lau and banker Lam Kwong-siu. Separately, acting housing secretary Michael Wong said on Commercial Radio that deciding the long-term future of the Wang Fuk Court site could take years: the government has said the land will be used for community facilities or a park rather than redevelopment, but consolidating ownership and demolishing the blocks will take time. He would not say whether a memorial park will be built.
stories.why: Two days after the first anniversary of a fire that killed 168 people, the honour recognises a firefighter’s sacrifice while families are still waiting to learn what happens to the site. Decisions about any memorial will be watched closely by survivors and families.

stories.headline: Taiwan local elections: KMT mayor leads China critic Puma Shen in Taipei count as the opposition claims early wins
stories.deck: Taiwan voted on Saturday, Nov. 28, in “nine-in-one” local elections for about 11,000 posts. With counting under way, official Central Election Commission figures at 7:18 p.m. Taipei time showed Kuomintang (KMT) Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an ahead of the governing Democratic Progressive Party’s Puma Shen by about 455,000 votes to 385,000, according to Focus Taiwan.
stories.summary: Taiwan voted on Saturday, Nov. 28, in “nine-in-one” local elections for about 11,000 posts. With counting under way, official Central Election Commission figures at 7:18 p.m. Taipei time showed Kuomintang (KMT) Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an ahead of the governing Democratic Progressive Party’s Puma Shen by about 455,000 votes to 385,000, according to Focus Taiwan, which said Shen appeared set to fall well short. Shen, an academic-turned-lawmaker and expert on Chinese information warfare, is wanted by Chinese police for “separatism,” Al Jazeera notes. In New Taipei, the KMT’s Lee Shu-chuan led the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui 50.70% to 48.75% in the official count. By 7:16 p.m., KMT candidates had declared victory in Kinmen, Lienchiang, Miaoli, Keelung, Nantou and Taitung, and the DPP’s Chou Chun-mi in Pingtung. A referendum on nuclear power was held alongside the vote; its result had not been reported in the sources checked.
stories.why: Local elections are read as a test of President William Lai’s DPP ahead of the 2028 presidential race, and of how voters weigh pressure from Beijing. A DPP loss in Taipei after a high-profile campaign by a China critic would be welcomed in Beijing, while the KMT’s strength in the cities sets the tone for the next two years.

stories.headline: China’s industrial profits jump 20.1% in October, led by AI-linked electronics while consumer manufacturers struggle
stories.deck: Profits at China’s larger industrial companies rose 20.1% in October from a year earlier, up from 14.4% in September and the fastest pace since May, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Friday, Nov. 27 (Beijing time).
stories.summary: Profits at China’s larger industrial companies rose 20.1% in October from a year earlier, up from 14.4% in September and the fastest pace since May, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Friday, Nov. 27 (Beijing time). Profits for the first ten months were up 16%. The gains were lopsided: Reuters, via RTHK, reports profits in computer, telecom and other electronics manufacturing doubled over the ten months while furniture makers’ fell 52.4%, and CNBC says growth was concentrated in sectors tied to the global AI build-out or higher commodity prices, while consumer-facing manufacturers struggled to pass on rising costs. The figures cover firms with annual revenue of at least 20 million yuan.
stories.why: The headline number looks strong, but it is being carried by AI hardware and energy, not by Chinese households. With domestic demand weak and new U.S. tariffs looming, the rebound depends heavily on exports and one tech boom.

stories.deck: Exiled activists say China’s economic and soft-power rise is pushing human-rights concerns down other governments’ agendas, in a BBC report published on Nov. 27.

Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, a former president of the World Uyghur Congress who has lived in Germany for nearly three decades, told the BBC that protests that drew thousands in 2018 now struggle to attract 500. Activists also told the BBC that Beijing has offered family reunions, money and promises of safety in exchange for information about their networks and for promoting party narratives; the Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed claims that exiles were asked to spy on one another. stories.headline: Liberals’ Jess Wilson wins Victoria’s state election, ending 12 years of Labor government; premier Ben Carroll loses his own seat
stories.deck: Liberal leader Jess Wilson will become premier of the Australian state of Victoria after the Liberal-National Coalition defeated Labor in Saturday’s election, ending 12 years of Labor rule, ABC News reports.
stories.summary: Liberal leader Jess Wilson will become premier of the Australian state of Victoria after the Liberal-National Coalition defeated Labor in Saturday’s election, ending 12 years of Labor rule, ABC News reports. Premier Ben Carroll, who took over the Labor leadership about four months ago, conceded before 8:30 p.m. local time and lost his own seat of Niddrie, the ABC says. “It’s not the result we wanted but it is a result we accept,” he said. Wilson, 36, will be the state’s first popularly elected female premier; she campaigned on potholes, crime and state debt, and days before the vote announced plans to partly privatise Melbourne’s sewerage network and scale back some Labor programmes. SBS reported that whether the Coalition wins an outright majority was still uncertain as counting continued.
stories.why: Victoria has long been a Labor stronghold, so losing it is a warning for the federal Labor government and shows voters punishing incumbents over debt and cost of living. Whether Wilson governs alone or needs crossbench support will shape how far her privatisation plans go.

stories.headline: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie convicted of manslaughter over 123 more Shakahola starvation deaths
stories.deck: A Kenyan High Court judge in Mombasa on Friday, Nov. 27, found self-styled pastor Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 adult followers he ordered to fast to death in Shakahola forest between 2021 and 2023.
stories.summary: A Kenyan High Court judge in Mombasa on Friday, Nov. 27, found self-styled pastor Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 adult followers he ordered to fast to death in Shakahola forest between 2021 and 2023. Judge Alex Ithuku also convicted 29 others, including Mackenzie’s wife, and acquitted 60; prosecutors said they would appeal the acquittals. Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing. Kenya’s prosecutors called Friday’s verdict “the final conviction” in the cases against him and said he had “systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died.” More than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves after his 2023 arrest. One of his lawyers said he would appeal, Reuters reported, according to the BBC.
stories.why: The verdict closes the main criminal cases over one of the world’s deadliest cult tragedies, but the acquittals and appeals mean it is not over for families. It also keeps pressure on Kenya over how it oversees fringe churches.
